Narrative Arc
NAIR-uh-tiv ark
noun phrase (biblical hermeneutics / literary theology)
Latin narrativus (relating to narration, from narrare, to recount) + Latin arcus (bow, arch; a curved line); the compound — drawn from literary analysis — names the overarching structure of Scripture as a single, unified story with a beginning (creation), a complicating event (the fall), a redemptive movement (the covenantal history of promise and fulfillment), and a climax and resolution in Christ and the new creation.

Biblical Definition

The narrative arc of Scripture is the unified, purposeful story that stretches from Genesis 1 to Revelation 22 — a single account of God's purposes in creation, the catastrophic rupture of the fall, the long covenantal movement of redemption through Israel, the incarnation and atoning work of Christ as the story's center and climax, and the consummation of all things in the new creation. The framework is not a literary abstraction imposed on the text from outside but the shape the canonical authors themselves declare the story to have.

Isaiah 46:10 establishes that God declares “the end from the beginning, and from ancient times things that are not yet done” — the God who speaks Scripture holds the whole arc in His sovereign view and reveals its shape progressively to His servants the prophets. Christ in Luke 24:27 reads the entire Old Testament as a unified, anticipatory testimony: “beginning with Moses and with all the prophets, He explained to them the things concerning Himself in all the Scriptures.” The Old Testament is not a disconnected anthology of religious writings but a single, coherent prologue to the story's fulfillment in Christ.

Paul's declaration that “as many as are the promises of God, in Him they are yes” (2Cor 1:20) identifies Christ as the hinge on which the entire narrative turns. The final chapter of the story is announced in the same terms as the first: “a new heaven and a new earth” (Rev 21:1), recalling creation and establishing the consummation as genuine re-creation rather than mere escape from the material world.

Webster 1828 Definition

Narrative arc: the overarching, unified story-structure of the 66-book biblical canon — beginning in creation, disrupted by the fall, progressively unfolding through covenantal redemption, reaching its climax and center in Christ's person and work, and moving toward consummation in the new creation; the shape of Scripture that the canonical authors themselves declare and that Christ confirms in Luke 24:27.

NARRATIVE ARC, noun phrase. The unified story-structure of the biblical canon from creation to new creation; the framework within which individual texts receive their fullest meaning.

Latin narrare (to relate, to tell a story) + arcus (arch, bow); the ‘arc’ metaphor captures the rising and falling shape of the story: creation, fall, redemptive movement, climax in Christ, consummation.

Distinct from allegorization: the narrative arc does not impose meanings on texts from outside but follows the linear movement of the canonical story as the biblical authors themselves present it, grounded in actual historical divine acts.

N. T. Wright's five-act drama model (creation, fall, Israel, Jesus, church) and Graeme Goldsworthy's kingdom-of-God framework are two Reformed-adjacent literary descriptions of the same biblical narrative arc; the underlying logic is the same: Scripture tells one story, and every part is understood in relation to the whole.

The Reformed confessional tradition grounds the narrative arc in the covenant of grace (1689 LBCF 7:2–3), which is the theological spine of the story: God's one redemptive purpose administered through successive covenant stages, all fulfilled in Christ.

Key Scripture

Isa 46:10 — "Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure:"

John 5:39 — "Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me."

Gen 12:3 — "And I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee: and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed."

Rev 22:20 — "He which testifieth these things saith, Surely I come quickly. Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus."

Modern Corruption

The primary modern corruptions of the narrative arc are (1) dispensational fragmentation, which breaks the story into disconnected segments with different governing principles; and (2) progressive Christianity's renarration, which treats the biblical narrative as a human story of moral evolution rather than the authoritative account of God's sovereign redemptive acts in history.

expand to see more

Dispensationalism's theological method requires fragmenting the biblical narrative arc into discrete, mutually discontinuous dispensations. On the most developed forms of the scheme (Darby, Scofield, Ryrie), Israel and the church have separate destinies, separate covenants, and essentially separate gospels; the kingdom announced in the Gospels was postponed because the Jews rejected Christ and will be reinstated in a literal millennial kingdom. This framework shatters the organic unity of the story that Christ Himself claimed in Luke 24 and that Hebrews 1:1–2 establishes: the many parts and many ways of the Old Testament speak in the one Son who is the appointed heir and consummation of all things. The dispensational fragmentation is not a minor interpretive variant; it restructures the entire redemptive narrative.

Progressive Christianity reimagines the narrative arc as the story of humanity's moral and spiritual evolution toward a more inclusive and compassionate social order — tracing a movement from tribal exclusivism toward universal welcome, from patriarchy toward egalitarianism. This is not the story Scripture tells about itself: the canonical narrative is not the story of human moral progress but the story of divine action against human rebellion — God calling, pursuing, redeeming, judging, and restoring a people for His own name and glory. Substituting a progressive social narrative for the covenantal-redemptive one renders Scripture a mirror for contemporary social ideals rather than a record of God's sovereign speaking and acting in history.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin roots naming the structure of extended narration and the curved shape that describes it; applied theologically to Scripture's unified story-shape, which the canonical authors themselves claim and which Christ confirms as the framework for reading all the Scriptures.

expand to see more

Latin narrare — to recount, to relate; from gnarus (knowing, familiar with); narration is the account given by someone who knows the events from within — Scripture's narrative is given by the God who declares the end from the beginning (Isa 46:10), making Him the ultimate first-person narrator of history

Latin arcus — arch, bow, arc; the physical image captures the shape of the biblical story: rising from creation, falling at the fall, arching upward through the redemptive history, reaching its apex at the resurrection of Christ, and descending into the new creation consummation

Greek euangelion — good news, gospel; the New Testament announcement that the narrative arc has reached its decisive turning point in Christ; the gospel is not a moral maxim but a story announcement: the promised One has come, the kingdom has broken in, the decisive victory has been won

Hebrew berith — covenant; the theological backbone of the narrative arc; each covenant stage (Noahic, Abrahamic, Mosaic, Davidic, new) is not a restart of the story but an advance of the same redemptive promise toward its fulfillment in Christ — the narrative arc is the story of the covenant of grace unfolding in history

Usage

"Reading any biblical text in its narrative-arc location is the prerequisite for faithful interpretation. A passage from Leviticus is not a free-floating religious instruction but a covenant-age regulation within the Mosaic administration of the covenant of grace; it faces forward toward the fulfillment in Christ (the Levitical priesthood as type of the Melchizedekian High Priest, Heb 7) and has its authority in the church age mediated through the New Testament's teaching on the continuity and discontinuity of the Mosaic covenant. The narrative location changes everything."

"Graeme Goldsworthy's framework in Gospel and Kingdom (1981) identifies the ‘kingdom of God’ pattern (God's people, in God's place, under God's rule) as the recurring thematic structure of the narrative arc from Eden to new Jerusalem. Each major covenant stage instantiates the pattern at a new level of fulfillment: the garden, Canaan, the temple, the church, the new creation — all are progressively realized expressions of the kingdom promise, giving the reader a canonical map for locating individual texts within the unified story."

"The proclamation of the gospel depends on the narrative arc: the “good news” is not a timeless moral principle but an announcement that a particular story has reached its promised turning point. Christ is “the yes” to all God's promises (2Cor 1:20) — not because He is a general religious principle but because He is the specific Person promised in the specific story that the entire Old Testament was telling. Remove the narrative arc and the gospel becomes a decontextualized slogan; restore it and the gospel becomes the announcement it is: the Promised One has come."
